traditions.name: Kolhapuri Chappal
traditions.tagline: A craft older than the runway.
alternateNames: Pie-taan / Paytaan (said to be an early name)
traditions.summary: Flat, open-toed, hand-stitched leather sandals made across eight districts of Maharashtra and Karnataka — and, in June 2025, the subject of one of fashion's most visible attribution debates.
traditions.intro: Long before it reached a Milan runway, the Kolhapuri chappal was everyday footwear: buffalo-hide leather, hand-stitched without nails, braided across the instep and finished with a loop for the big toe. Its name belongs to a city. Its making belongs to communities of leather-workers on both sides of the Maharashtra–Karnataka border.

origins.text: The chappal takes its name from Kolhapur, in southern Maharashtra, but it has never belonged to one town. The geographical indication registered for it covers eight districts: Kolhapur, Sangli, Satara and Solapur in Maharashtra, and Belagavi, Dharwad, Bagalkot and Vijayapura in Karnataka.

How old is it? Popular histories place its beginnings in the 12th–13th centuries, before it was called 'Kolhapuri' at all. Other accounts credit a single family with designing it in 1920. We have found no primary evidence for either date, so we show both — and mark them disputed.

Early forms are said to have gone by village names — Kapashi, Paytaan, Kachkadi, Bakkalnali, Pukri. These names survive in oral and journalistic accounts rather than in archives, and we record them as such.

The trade is widely said to have flourished under royal patronage in princely Kolhapur. Accounts disagree on which ruler and when; most point to Chhatrapati Shahu Maharaj in the early 20th century, with tanning centres opened under his rule.

origins.title: On names and ownership
origins.text: A geographical indication protects the use of a name — 'Kolhapuri Chappal' — for goods made in the registered area. It records a place-based reputation. It is not a patent, and it does not make anyone the worldwide owner of the open-toed sandal as a form.

significance.text: The chappal is valued for being made to last and made by hand: leather and thread, no nails, a form refined for heat and dust. Its name carries the reputation of a region; its price, at a roadside stall, has often been a few hundred rupees.
The design travelled in seconds. The name, the place and the makers took a week of public argument to catch up.

intro.text: Kolhapuri chappals are predominantly made — then and now — by Charmakar leather-working communities. The craft runs through tanning, cutting, braiding and stitching, often divided between households and workshops.

The material story is changing. Leather was traditionally vegetable-tanned in and around Kolhapur; reporting in 2025 found that many local tanneries had closed and makers now buy leather from elsewhere, often chemically tanned.

materials.name: Buffalo hide
materials.detail: The traditional leather. Cow hide has also been used, which is contested.

materials.name: Thread
materials.detail: Uppers and soles are hand-stitched; traditionally no nails are used.

materials.name: Vegetable tannins
materials.detail: Plant-based tanning was traditional; much leather today comes from tanneries using chemical processes.

process.title: Skiving
process.detail: Leather is thinned and evened for each part of the chappal.

process.title: Pattern & cutting
process.detail: Soles, straps and the toe loop are cut by hand from templates.

process.title: Layering the sole
process.detail: Sole layers and heel are built up and attached to the upper.

process.title: Stitching
process.detail: Parts are joined with thread — no nails.

process.title: Braiding & punching
process.detail: Strips are braided and punched into the decorative upper.

process.title: Finishing & polish
process.detail: Edges are trimmed, surfaces decorated and polished.

makers.voicesNote: We have not yet recorded interviews with Kolhapuri makers. Rather than paraphrase artisans from press coverage, this space stays empty until makers choose to speak for themselves here.

timeline.title: An origin before the name
timeline.body: Popular histories place the chappal's beginnings here, before it was called 'Kolhapuri'. A competing account credits a single family with the design in 1920. Neither claim rests on evidence we could verify.

timeline.title: Royal patronage in princely Kolhapur
timeline.body: Accounts credit the rulers of Kolhapur — most often Chhatrapati Shahu Maharaj — with encouraging the trade and opening tanning centres. Which ruler, and when, needs archival confirmation.

timeline.title: A joint GI application
timeline.body: An application to register 'Kolhapuri Chappal' as a geographical indication is filed (No. 169), covering districts in both Maharashtra and Karnataka. Some secondary sources give 4 April 2009.

timeline.title: Behind museum glass in Toronto
timeline.body: A late-20th-century chappal from Kolhapur is photographed on display at the Bata Shoe Museum — the craft named and placed in a museum, years before the runway.

timeline.title: Advertised in the GI Journal
timeline.body: The application is published in GI Journal No. 109, listing four districts in each state as the area of production.

timeline.title: Registered as a geographical indication
timeline.body: The registry records certificate No. 329 for Kolhapuri Chappal. News of the registration was widely reported in mid-2019.

timeline.title: The Milan runway
timeline.body: Prada's Men's Spring/Summer 2026 show in Milan features open-toed leather sandals. Show notes call them 'leather sandals' and make no reference to India.

timeline.title: Acknowledgement after criticism
timeline.body: After criticism from artisans, designers and Maharashtra's chamber of commerce, Prada acknowledges in a letter that the sandals were inspired by traditional Indian handcrafted footwear.

timeline.title: A visit to the workshops
timeline.body: A Prada technical team visits Kolhapur's chappal-making cluster, observes production and meets artisans.

timeline.title: A court declines to decide
timeline.body: The Bombay High Court dismisses a public interest litigation against Prada, questioning the petitioners' standing and leaving registered GI proprietors free to pursue remedies. It makes no finding on infringement.

timeline.title: An agreement with the GI proprietors
timeline.body: Prada signs a memorandum of understanding in Mumbai with LIDCOM (Maharashtra) and LIDKAR (Karnataka) for a limited-edition sandal collection made in India. Reports differ on whether it was signed on 10 or 11 December.

timeline.title: 'Made in India x Inspired by Kolhapuri Chappals'
timeline.body: Prada announces the collection — reported as about 2,000 pairs made by artisans in Maharashtra and Karnataka — with a three-year training programme for 180 artisans.

intro.text: Inspiration is not the problem. Footwear has always borrowed across borders, and a sandal can be admired in Milan as easily as in Kolhapur. What this chapter documents is narrower: the moment when a recognisable design travelled and its name, place and makers did not.

influences.title: A museum object abroad
influences.body: A late-20th-century Kolhapur chappal was displayed at the Bata Shoe Museum in Toronto, labelled by place.

influences.title: Heritage pride after the runway
influences.body: In the weeks after the Prada debate, Indian brands and sellers leaned on the chappal's heritage in their own marketing.

cases.title: The runway, Milan, June 2025
cases.summary: Open-toed leather sandals in Prada's Men's Spring/Summer 2026 show were widely recognised as Kolhapuri in style, but presented as 'leather sandals'. After public criticism Prada acknowledged the Indian inspiration, visited Kolhapur, signed an agreement with the GI proprietors and, in 2026, released a collection made in India.

events.title: A regional craft
events.body: Hand-stitched leather chappals are made by Charmakar communities across southern Maharashtra and northern Karnataka.

events.title: The name is protected
events.body: 'Kolhapuri Chappal' is registered as a geographical indication for eight districts in two states.

events.title: Shown as 'leather sandals'
events.body: The sandals appear on the Milan runway; the show notes make no reference to India.

events.title: Public concern
events.body: Artisans, designers and politicians in India object to the missing credit; Maharashtra's chamber of commerce writes to the company.

events.title: Acknowledgement
events.body: Prada's head of corporate social responsibility replies that the design was inspired by traditional Indian handcrafted footwear.

events.title: From acknowledgement to agreement
events.body: A technical team visits Kolhapur; a court declines a public-interest case on standing; an MoU is signed with LIDCOM and LIDKAR; a made-in-India collection and artisan training programme follow.

travelled: The toe loop and T-strap arrangement
The braided leather band across the foot
leftBehind: The difference between a roadside price and a runway price

questions.a: An open-toed, flat leather sandal with a toe loop and braided upper — the features observers in India and abroad immediately read as Kolhapuri.

questions.q: What was the traditional cultural context?
questions.a: Hand-stitched footwear made predominantly by Charmakar leather-workers in four districts of Maharashtra and four of Karnataka, protected as a geographical indication since 2018–19.

questions.q: How was the design described commercially?
questions.a: As 'leather sandals'. The show notes did not mention India, Kolhapur or the people who make the form.
Not at first. Prada acknowledged the inspiration in a letter only after public criticism, in late June 2025.

Not in the runway design. Afterwards a Prada team visited Kolhapur's workshops (July 2025), and the 2026 collection was reported as made by artisans in Maharashtra and Karnataka under an agreement with the two state corporations.

An acknowledgement, a workshop visit, an MoU with the GI proprietors, a product named for the tradition, and a funded three-year training programme for 180 artisans with NIFT and KILT among the partners. How its benefits reach individual makers is not yet documented.

legalNote.text: No court has ruled that Prada infringed the geographical indication. The Bombay High Court dismissed a public interest litigation because the petitioners were not the registered proprietors; it left LIDCOM and LIDKAR free to act. A GI protects the use of a name for goods from a registered area — it does not by itself grant worldwide rights over a sandal design.

adaptation.title: Runway interpretation, June 2025
points: No reference to India in show notes
adaptation.mediaNote: We have not licensed runway photography, so we will not reproduce it. Editors can attach a properly licensed image from the admin. Until then, see the photo galleries in the linked press coverage.

openQuestions: How are proceeds or training places distributed among makers outside the LIDCOM and LIDKAR networks?
Will future collections credit the tradition by name at the moment of first presentation?
Do makers themselves consider the outcome adequate? We have not yet asked them directly.

claims.text: The Kolhapuri Chappal geographical indication covers Kolhapur, Sangli, Satara and Solapur districts in Maharashtra and Belagavi, Dharwad, Bagalkot and Vijayapura (Bijapur) districts in Karnataka.
The GI application (No. 169) was filed on 4 May 2009; the registry records certificate No. 329 dated 11 December 2018. The registration was widely reported in mid-2019.
claims.note: Some sources give 4 April 2009 as the filing date; several date the grant to June–July 2019, when it was publicised.

claims.text: Court reporting identifies LIDCOM (Maharashtra) and LIDKAR (Karnataka) as the registered proprietors of the GI; the registry's public record names the Central Leather Research Institute as applicant.
claims.note: The two records are not necessarily in conflict (an institution may file for proprietors), but we have not seen the certificate itself.

claims.text: The chappal's origins are often placed in the 12th–13th centuries; another account attributes its design to the Saudagar family in 1920.
claims.note: Neither date is supported by a primary source we could find. Open presents the early date as belief; Wikipedia's 1920 claim is uncited.

claims.text: Early forms are said to have been known as Kapashi, Paytaan, Kachkadi, Bakkalnali and Pukri, after the villages where they were made.
claims.note: Reported as tradition ('is said to'); meanings of the names are not recorded in our sources.

claims.text: Accounts credit the rulers of Kolhapur with encouraging the trade: Wikipedia names Shahu I and his successor Rajaram II and counts 29 tanning centres opened in Shahu's reign; Open Magazine places Shahu Maharaj's patronage in the early 20th century.
claims.note: Wikipedia links this to 'Shahu I' and successors and cites 29 tanning centres from 2019 newspaper features; Open places patronage in the early 20th century. Which ruler, and when, needs archival confirmation.

claims.text: Kolhapuri chappals are predominantly made by Charmakar leather-working communities.
claims.note: Other community names appear in commercial sources but are not yet verified. Community self-identification will be recorded in consultation with makers.

claims.text: Kolhapuri chappals are traditionally made from buffalo hide and thread, hand-stitched without nails.

Kolhapuri leather was known for local vegetable tanning; by 2025 most tanneries in the city had shut after a crackdown on effluents, and makers relied mainly on tanneries in Tamil Nadu that use chemical processes.
claims.note: Wikipedia still describes local vegetable tanning; Open's 2025 reporting is more recent.

claims.text: Press coverage set a pair bargained for about ₹400 at a Delhi market against Prada's sandal at about ₹1 lakh; Prada's 2026 made-in-India edition was reported at about €750 (roughly ₹83,000).

resources.note: The primary public record of the Kolhapuri Chappal geographical indication.

resources.title: 'Prada Wears Kolhapuri' — Open Magazine
resources.note: Long-form reporting from Kolhapur's workshops and markets, 2025.

collaborationNotes: Name the tradition — 'Kolhapuri chappal' — wherever the design is shown, from the first presentation.
Only goods made in the eight registered districts can carry the Kolhapuri Chappal name.
Work through the GI proprietors and makers' organisations, and agree on fair payment and credit before production.
Link this passport, or its QR code, beside the product so its story travels with it.

related.reason: Another tradition that met fashion — in a museum exhibition that placed phulkari beside designer garments.
Also from Maharashtra. Its GI was pursued by an Adivasi organisation after its imagery circulated online without context.
A hand process — block, dye, wash, repeat — whose rising demand is changing the craft that makes it.

traditions.name: Madhubani Painting
traditions.tagline: From the walls of a wedding room to the walls of the world.

nativeNames.note: Mithila painting

places.note: District that gives the painting its best-known name

traditions.summary: A painting tradition of the Mithila region — northern Bihar and neighbouring Nepal — made for centuries by women on the walls of homes, and carried onto paper and into the world in the 20th century.
traditions.intro: Mithila painting began as something made for a room and an occasion: a wedding chamber, a festival, a threshold. Women drew gods, fish, birds and lotus vines in dense double lines. When the world met it, first through a colonial officer's camera and then through paper sold in Delhi, its makers' names travelled more slowly than its images.

origins.text: Madhubani is a district; Mithila is a region. The painting carries both names, and the region it comes from spans northern Bihar in India and the adjoining Madhesh of Nepal, around Janakpur. This passport is listed under both countries for that reason.

It was painted by women, on the walls and floors of homes, for rituals and especially weddings. A widely told story traces it to the Ramayana — to King Janaka asking for his palace to be painted for the wedding of his daughter Sita. We record that as tradition, not history.

Outsiders' accounts begin with disaster. After the 1934 Bihar–Nepal earthquake, the British officer William G. Archer saw paintings exposed on the inner walls of damaged houses; he returned to photograph them and published an article in the journal Marg in 1949.

origins.title: Whose story was told first?
origins.text: Scholars note that Archer's framing centred Brahmin and Kayastha painting and overlooked other communities' traditions. A history that begins with the person who 'discovered' an art form is one of the gaps this archive exists to close.

In the drought of the mid-1960s, the All India Handicrafts Board — under Pupul Jayakar, with the artist-officer Bhaskar Kulkarni — encouraged women to paint on paper so their work could be sold. Wall painting became portable, and Mithila painters began to be known by name.

significance.text: Commonly described styles include bharni (filled colour), kachni (fine line), tantrik, godna and kohbar — the last named for the painted wedding chamber. These are classifications used by practitioners and scholars, and the boundaries between them are not fixed.
The painting left the wall in the 1960s. The painters' names took decades to follow.

intro.text: Mithila painting has been a women's art, and its best-known practitioners — honoured nationally since the 1970s — are women. The Padma Shri, one of India's highest civilian honours, has gone to Jagdamba Devi, Sita Devi, Ganga Devi, Mahasundari Devi, Baua Devi and Dulari Devi, among others.

materials.name: Wall and floor
materials.detail: The original surfaces: plastered walls and floors of homes, renewed for occasions.

materials.name: Paper
materials.detail: Introduced for sale during the 1960s drought programme; now the most common support.

materials.name: Natural pigments
materials.detail: Traditionally plant- and mineral-based colours; practices vary by painter and period.

process.title: Border first
process.detail: Compositions are commonly framed with a decorated border.

process.title: Double outline
process.detail: Figures are drawn in double lines, filled with hatching (kachni) or colour (bharni).

process.title: No empty ground
process.detail: Spaces are filled with flowers, fish, birds and geometric pattern.

practitioners.name: Jagdamba Devi
practitioners.note: Padma Shri, 1975 — the first Mithila painter to receive it.

makers.voicesNote: The names above are public honours. We have not recorded interviews, and we do not attribute quotations to painters from secondary sources.

timeline.title: Painting for Sita's wedding
timeline.body: In the widely told story, King Janaka has his kingdom painted for his daughter Sita's wedding. It is a tradition about origins, not a dated event.

timeline.title: Revealed by an earthquake
timeline.body: After the Bihar–Nepal earthquake, W. G. Archer sees paintings on the exposed inner walls of damaged homes, and later photographs them.

timeline.title: 'Maithil painting' in Marg
timeline.body: Archer's article in Marg brings the painting to scholarly attention — and shapes how it is classified for decades.

timeline.title: From walls to paper
timeline.body: During a severe drought, the All India Handicrafts Board encourages women to paint on paper for sale. Some sources date the start of the programme to 1964.

timeline.title: A painter named nationally
timeline.body: Jagdamba Devi becomes the first Mithila painter to receive the Padma Shri.

timeline.title: A museum in snowy Niigata
timeline.body: Tokio Hasegawa opens the Mithila Museum in Tokamachi, Japan, in a converted elementary school. It grows into one of the largest collections of Mithila painting anywhere.

timeline.title: Registered as a geographical indication
timeline.body: 'Madhubani Paintings' is registered as a GI for Bihar, on an application by the state's Director of Industries filed in 2005.

intro.text: Few Indian painting traditions have travelled further: to Delhi's craft markets, to Japanese museum walls, to railway stations and printed merchandise. The question here is not whether it should travel, but whether the women who made it travel with it.

influences.title: A collection in Japan
influences.body: The Mithila Museum in Tokamachi has collected and exhibited Mithila painting since 1982 — one of the clearest cases of an outside institution building a relationship with a tradition over decades.

influences.title: Painting on public walls
influences.body: Madhubani railway station's walls carry large Mithila paintings, photographed in 2021.

influences.title: Printed copies and authenticity
influences.body: Commentators argue that printed reproductions sold as 'Madhubani' undercut hand painters, and that GI protection has been weakly enforced.

claims.text: Madhubani (Mithila) painting comes from the Mithila region, which spans northern Bihar in India and adjoining parts of Nepal.
It was traditionally painted by women on the walls and floors of homes, especially for rituals and weddings.
A widely told origin story links the painting to King Janaka commissioning paintings for the wedding of his daughter Sita.
claims.note: An origin legend, recorded as tradition.

claims.text: After the 1934 Bihar–Nepal earthquake, William G. Archer saw paintings on the inner walls of damaged houses, later photographed them, and published an article in Marg in 1949.
Archer's framing centred Brahmin and Kayastha styles and overlooked other communities' painting.

During the drought of the mid-1960s the All India Handicrafts Board (called the Handloom Board in some accounts), under Pupul Jayakar and with Bhaskar Kulkarni, encouraged women to paint on paper for sale.
claims.note: Sources differ on whether the intervention began in 1964 or 1966–68.

claims.text: Commonly named styles include bharni, kachni, tantrik, godna and kohbar.

Mithila painters who have received the Padma Shri include Jagdamba Devi (1975), Sita Devi (1981), Ganga Devi (1984), Mahasundari Devi (2011), Baua Devi (2017), Godawari Dutta (2019) and Dulari Devi (2021).
claims.note: One outlet gives 2010 for Mahasundari Devi, and Wikipedia gives 2020 for Dulari Devi; the 2021 Padma list (announced 25 January 2021) names her.

claims.text: 'Madhubani Paintings' was registered as a geographical indication for Bihar (certificate dated 16 May 2007) on an application by Bihar's Director of Industries.
claims.note: The record shows validity to 21 August 2025 and a 2024 renewal notice; current renewal status is not confirmed.

claims.text: The Mithila Museum in Tokamachi, Niigata, Japan, was founded by Tokio Hasegawa and inaugurated in 1982; Hasegawa had converted an elementary school there into a centre for the collection.
claims.note: Reported collection sizes vary from about 850 to over 3,000 works.

resources.note: Essays and interviews on the painting's history and its historiography.

Don't sell printed reproductions as hand painting.

related.reason: Another wall painting tradition that moved onto paper in the 1960s–70s and made individual painters famous.
Also a women's art made for weddings, and also divided by a modern border.

traditions.name: Phulkari
traditions.tagline: Flower work, stitched from the back.
traditions.summary: Embroidery of undivided Punjab — silk floss darned into hand-woven cotton from the reverse — made by women for weddings and family life, on both sides of a border drawn in 1947.
traditions.intro: Phulkari means flower work. It was made by women in Punjab, a region that since 1947 has been divided between India and Pakistan. Untwisted silk floss is darned into hand-woven cotton from the back of the cloth, so the pattern appears on the front: sometimes scattered flowers, sometimes — in a bagh, a 'garden' — the whole cloth covered.

origins.text: Phulkari belongs to Punjab — a region now divided between India and Pakistan. It was made on both sides of today's border, which is why this passport is filed under India but listed under Pakistan too.
How old is it? Sources disagree, and we have not found reliable dating for its beginnings. What is well documented is how it was made and used by the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
Partition in 1947 divided Punjab and scattered the households, neighbours and merchants — sellers of hand-woven khaddar and silk floss — on whom the embroidery depended.

significance.text: Phulkari and bagh were made for family and ceremony, above all weddings. Some pieces were embroidered for a bride and carried with her into a new household.

intro.text: Phulkari is women's work, made at home and often together. Its technique turns the cloth into a counting grid: stitches are darned on the reverse, following the weave of the khaddar, so the pattern is built thread by thread.

materials.name: Pat
materials.detail: Untwisted silk floss, traditionally golden, white, crimson and other bright colours.

materials.name: Khaddar
materials.detail: Hand-spun, hand-woven cotton cloth, often dyed earth-red or brown.

process.title: Count the weave
process.detail: The design follows the threads of the khaddar rather than a drawn outline.

process.title: Darn from the back
process.detail: Long and short darning stitches are worked on the reverse so the pattern shows on the front.

process.title: Fill the garden
process.detail: In a bagh, darning covers almost the whole ground of the cloth.

makers.voicesNote: We have not yet recorded embroiderers' own accounts. Museum catalogues describe many historic phulkari as made by anonymous women — a gap this passport will not fill by inventing names.

timeline.title: Origins we cannot yet date
timeline.body: Claims about phulkari's age vary widely. We have not found a reliable source for when it began.

timeline.title: A portrait in phulkari
timeline.body: A photograph from Patiala shows a woman draped in phulkari — an archival glimpse of how it was worn.

timeline.title: Punjab divided
timeline.body: Partition separates the region and disrupts the networks that sustained the embroidery.

timeline.title: A GI application
timeline.body: Punjab Small Industries & Export Corporation applies to register Phulkari as a geographical indication for Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan.

timeline.title: Registered
timeline.body: The registry issues certificate No. 145. Many secondary sources date this to 2011.

timeline.title: Philadelphia
timeline.body: The Philadelphia Museum of Art opens what was described as the first major US exhibition of phulkari, including its losses at Partition and its use in contemporary fashion.

intro.text: Phulkari has travelled into museums and into fashion, often at the same time. Its story is also one of a border: an embroidery that belongs to a region now split between two countries.

influences.title: Museum and runway, side by side
influences.body: The 2017 Philadelphia exhibition placed historic phulkari beside contemporary garments that use the embroidery.

influences.title: A protected name with low awareness
influences.body: Reporting found that few producers in Punjab and Haryana were aware of, or benefiting from, the GI.

claims.text: Phulkari is an embroidery tradition of Punjab, a region now divided between India and Pakistan.
The date of phulkari's origin is not established.
claims.note: Secondary sources variously cite medieval or 15th-century origins; we found no reliable evidence for either.

claims.text: Phulkari is worked in untwisted silk floss (pat) on hand-woven cotton (khaddar), mainly in darning stitch from the reverse of the cloth.
Phulkari and bagh were made for family and ceremonial use, especially weddings.
The 1947 Partition disrupted the communities and trade networks that sustained phulkari.
Phulkari was registered as a GI for Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan (certificate dated 22 October 2010) on an application by the Punjab Small Industries & Export Corporation.
claims.note: Many secondary sources give 2011.

Another women's art made for weddings, and another region divided by a modern border.
Another tradition that met global fashion — and the question of credit.

traditions.name: Warli Painting
traditions.tagline: A circle, a triangle, a community.
traditions.summary: The ritual wall painting of the Warli Adivasi community of the Maharashtra–Gujarat border — now one of India's most reproduced visual languages, and one of its least credited.
traditions.intro: Figures made of two triangles and a circle; dancers spiralling around a musician; fields, animals and spirits on an earthen wall. Warli painting belongs to the Warli community. It is now printed on mugs and murals far from Dahanu — often without the community's name.

origins.text: Warli painting is the wall painting of the Warli (Varli) people, an Adivasi community of the coastal and hill districts along the Maharashtra–Gujarat border. Its registered geographical area spans Maharashtra, Gujarat, Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu.

Accounts describe white paint of rice flour and water on mud walls, often over red ochre or cow dung, and a vocabulary of circles, triangles, squares and lines. This draft has not yet been reviewed with Warli painters, so these descriptions are marked for verification.

significance.text: Ritual meaning, the names of motifs and who may paint what are questions this passport will answer only with the community. Until then, we describe what is publicly documented and leave the rest open.

intro.text: The best-documented Warli painter is Jivya Soma Mashe, who took the painting onto paper and canvas and exhibited internationally. He received the Padma Shri in 2011 and died in Dahanu in 2018.

materials.name: Rice paste
materials.detail: Described as the traditional white pigment.

materials.name: Earthen wall
materials.detail: Walls prepared with mud and cow dung form the ground.

practitioners.name: Jivya Soma Mashe (d. 2018)
practitioners.note: Exhibited at 'Magiciens de la Terre', Paris, 1989; Padma Shri 2011.

makers.voicesNote: Editorial draft. No interviews have been recorded; we will not publish process details until Warli painters have reviewed them.

timeline.title: Painting for ritual
timeline.body: Warli painting is described as ritual wall painting, renewed for occasions. Its age is not documented in our sources.

timeline.title: Paris

intro.text: Warli's simple geometry makes it easy to copy, and it is copied everywhere. Reporting suggests that this — images circulating online without context — is part of why a community organisation went to the trouble of registering it.

influences.title: Exhibited as contemporary art
influences.body: Warli painting entered international contemporary-art exhibitions through Jivya Soma Mashe, beginning with Paris in 1989.

claims.text: Warli painting is the wall painting of the Warli Adivasi community, centred on Dahanu, Talasari, Jawhar, Palghar and Mokhada in northern Maharashtra; the GI also covers Gujarat, Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu.
Warli painting is traditionally made in white paint of rice flour and water on mud walls, often over red ochre (geru) or cow dung, using circles, triangles, squares and lines.

claims.text: Jivya Soma Mashe exhibited at 'Magiciens de la Terre' (Centre Pompidou, 1989), received the Padma Shri in 2011, and died in Dahanu on 15 May 2018.

traditions.name: Ajrakh
traditions.tagline: Indigo and madder, printed on both sides of a border.
traditions.summary: A resist-printed, naturally dyed cloth shared by Sindh in Pakistan and Kutch and Barmer in India, carried across the region by Khatri printing families.
traditions.intro: Ajrakh is printed, washed, dyed, printed again — in indigo, madder red, black and white, in repeating stars and lattices. It is worn in Sindh, printed in Kutch and Barmer, and claimed by many origin stories at once. This passport is an editorial draft: it records what is documented and marks the rest.

origins.text: Ajrakh is shared. It is made and worn in Sindh, in Pakistan, and printed in Kutch in Gujarat and in Barmer in Rajasthan. The geographical indication registered in India in 2024 covers Kutch Ajrakh only; it says nothing about ajrak from Sindh.
It is associated with Khatri dyer-printer families. Popular histories say they came to Kutch from Sindh; accounts of when differ, from the 16th century to about 400 years ago.

origins.title: Similarity is not ancestry
origins.text: Ajrakh is often called '5,000 years old', linking it to the trefoil-patterned robe of the Mohenjo-daro 'priest-king' sculpture. That link rests on visual similarity alone. No textile evidence connects the two, and this archive does not present resemblance as proof of descent.
Even the name is contested: printers explain it as 'aaj rakh' — keep it today — while others connect it to the Arabic azraq, blue.

intro.text: After the 2001 Kutch earthquake, many printing families moved from Dhamadka to a new settlement near Bhuj — Ajrakhpur — which now holds the registered proprietor of the GI.

An oral-history interview with master printer Dr Ismail Mohammad Khatri, recorded for the University of Warwick, is the best first-person account we can point to. We link to it rather than paraphrase him.

intro.text: Ajrakh's patterns now appear in fashion far from Kutch and Sindh, both hand-printed and digitally imitated. Reporting from Kutch describes how rising demand is changing the craft's economics.

influences.title: Demand and imitation
influences.body: Growing demand has changed the dynamics of the tradition behind the art, according to reporting from Bhuj.

claims.text: Ajrakh is a resist-printed, naturally dyed textile shared by Sindh (Pakistan) and Kutch and Barmer (India).
Ajrakh is associated with Khatri dyer-printer families, many of whom trace their origins to Sindh.

Accounts of when Khatri printers settled in Kutch differ: a popular history says they came from Sindh about 400 years ago, while a family oral history places the first settler in Dhamadka in the 16th century.
claims.note: Accounts differ on the date and on the reasons for the move.

claims.text: The name is explained as 'aaj rakh' ('keep it today') or linked to the Arabic azraq ('blue').
claims.note: Both are folk or popular etymologies; neither is established.

claims.text: After the 2001 Kutch earthquake, many printing families moved from Dhamadka to Ajrakhpur, near Bhuj.
claims.note: Sources also cite rising iron content in Dhamadka's water.

traditions.name: Al Sadu
traditions.tagline: Bands of black, white and red, woven on the ground.
alternateNames: Al Sadu, traditional weaving skills in the United Arab Emirates
traditions.summary: A traditional weaving of Bedouin women in the UAE's rural communities — spun on a drop spindle, woven on a floor loom, in narrow geometric bands — inscribed by UNESCO in 2011 and moved to its Representative List in New Delhi in 2025.
traditions.intro: Al Sadu is the first passport in the UAE collection, and the archive's bridge. Everything here comes from UNESCO's own decisions and from government heritage records, because an introduction should begin on firm ground.

origins.text: UNESCO describes Al Sadu as a traditional form of weaving practised by Bedouin women in rural communities of the United Arab Emirates. Men shear the sheep, camels and goats; women clean and prepare the wool, spin it, dye it and weave it.
Its colours are black, white, brown, beige and red, in narrow bands of geometric design. Woven pieces furnish homes and tents and dress camels and horses.

significance.text: Weaving was also a social occasion. Gatherings of weavers are the traditional means of passing the skill on: girls learn by watching, then by sorting wool, before they are trusted with the loom.

intro.text: In 2011 UNESCO judged the skill to be at risk — its know-how kept by a dwindling number of older women. Fourteen years of safeguarding later, it was moved to the Representative List and the UAE's programme was selected as a good practice for others to learn from.

materials.name: Sheep, camel and goat hair
materials.detail: Shorn by men, cleaned and prepared by women.

materials.name: Plant dyes
materials.detail: Colours extracted from plants; access to natural dyes has been a safeguarding concern.

process.title: Shear
process.detail: Men shear sheep, camels and goats.

process.title: Clean & prepare
process.detail: Women clean and prepare the wool.

process.title: Spin
process.detail: Yarn is spun on a drop spindle.

process.title: Dye
process.detail: Yarn is dyed with colours extracted from plants.

process.title: Weave
process.detail: Weaving on a floor loom in a warp-faced plain weave, in narrow geometric bands.

makers.voicesNote: No weavers' accounts are published here yet. The UAE collection will add them only with consent and verification.

timeline.body: UNESCO inscribes Al Sadu on the List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding.

timeline.title: A report, and advice
timeline.body: UNESCO's committee invites the UAE to teach Al Sadu in schools, secure raw materials and natural dyeing, and watch for over-commercialisation.

timeline.title: A sister craft inscribed
timeline.body: Al Talli, the UAE's traditional braided embroidery, joins UNESCO's Representative List.

timeline.title: New Delhi
timeline.body: Meeting in New Delhi, UNESCO's committee transfers Al Sadu to the Representative List and selects the UAE's safeguarding programme for the Register of Good Safeguarding Practices.

intro.text: UNESCO itself has warned about over-commercialisation: Sadu patterns are now printed on goods far from the loom. As the UAE collection grows, this chapter will document how those patterns travel.

influences.title: India and the UAE, in one decision
influences.body: The decision moving Al Sadu to the Representative List was taken at UNESCO's 20th committee session, held in New Delhi in December 2025.

claims.text: Al Sadu is a traditional weaving practised by Bedouin women in rural communities of the UAE.
Men shear sheep, camels and goats; women clean and prepare the wool, spin it on a drop spindle, dye it and weave it on a floor loom in a warp-faced plain weave.
Traditional colours are black, white, brown, beige and red, in narrow bands of geometric design.
Al Sadu is used for soft furnishings and for decorative accessories for camels and horses.
Girls learn by watching and by tasks such as sorting wool; gatherings of weavers are the traditional means of transmission.
UNESCO inscribed Al Sadu on the Urgent Safeguarding List in 2011.
In 2020 UNESCO invited the UAE to integrate Al Sadu into school teaching, address access to raw materials and natural dyeing, and heed the risk of over-commercialisation.
In December 2025, in New Delhi, UNESCO transferred Al Sadu to the Representative List and selected the UAE's safeguarding programme for the Register of Good Safeguarding Practices.

traditions.name: Kente cloth
traditions.summary: Ghanaian fabric made of strips that are woven from silk, cotton or rayon using horizontal looms.
traditions.intro: Ghanaian fabric made of strips that are woven from silk, cotton or rayon using horizontal looms.

origins.text: Kente is a Ghanaian textile of narrow hand-woven strips of silk and cotton sewn together, now protected as a geographical indication of Ghana. It was traditionally worn wrapped like a toga by the Asante, Akan and Ewe peoples; Asante tradition places its origin in Bonwire in the Ashanti Region. Today it is worn widely for special occasions.

It is listed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in the element “Craftsmanship of traditional woven textile Kente” (inscribed 2024, as recorded on Wikidata).

origins.text: Dainichido Bugaku is a yearly set of sacred dances and music held at the Dainichido hall in Kazuno, Akita Prefecture. Tradition says court musicians taught the dances to local people in the early eighth century while the hall was being rebuilt. Seven dances are performed today, accompanied by flute and taiko, with masks including shishi and Vairocana.
It is listed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in the element “Dainichido Bugaku” (inscribed 2009, as recorded on Wikidata).

origins.text: The Gion Matsuri is one of Japan's largest festivals, held throughout July in Kyoto around the Yasaka Shrine in the Gion district. A Shinto festival, it began as a rite to purify the city and calm the forces thought to cause disease. It is best known for its two great processions of floats, the Yamaboko Junkō, on 17 and 24 July.
It is listed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in the element “Yama, Hoko, Yatai, float festivals in Japan” (inscribed 2016, as recorded on Wikidata).

traditions.intro: Culinary traditions of Japan.

origins.text: Washoku, the traditional cuisine of Japan, is built on rice and miso soup with side dishes that follow the seasons — fish, pickled vegetables and vegetables simmered in broth. Seafood may be grilled, served raw as sashimi or sushi, or fried in light tempura batter; noodles such as soba and udon are another staple.

It is listed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in the element “Washoku, traditional dietary cultures of the Japanese, notably for the celebration of New Year” (inscribed 2013, as recorded on Wikidata).

origins.text: Kumi odori is a form of narrative dance-theatre from the Ryukyu Kingdom, first presented in the capital, Shuri, in 1719 to entertain Chinese envoys. The courtier Tamagusuku Chokun is credited with establishing it. Drawing on several East Asian dance traditions, it remains part of Okinawan culture today.

It is listed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in the element “Kumiodori, traditional Okinawan musical theatre” (inscribed 2010, as recorded on Wikidata).

origins.text: Washi is Japanese paper made by hand from the inner bark of the gampi tree, the mitsumata shrub or the paper mulberry (kōzo). It is the paper of origami, calligraphy and ukiyo-e prints, and was once used for clothes, toys, household goods and ritual objects. Because it is tougher than wood-pulp paper, it is often used to repair historic books and artworks.

Thought to have begun among the Nahua, Huastec and Otomi peoples of central Mexico, it sees five men climb a pole about 30 metres high; four launch themselves off, tied by ropes, and circle down to the ground while the fifth dances and plays flute and drum at the top.
It is listed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in the element “Ritual ceremony of the Voladores” (inscribed 2009, as recorded on Wikidata).

traditions.intro: Form of traditional music from Mexico.

origins.text: Mariachi is a genre of regional Mexican music that grew up in the countryside of western Mexico from at least the 18th century. A typical group has up to eight violins, two trumpets and guitars — including the high vihuela and the deep guitarrón — and every player sings. Migration to Guadalajara and national cultural policy in the 19th and 20th centuries made it a symbol of Mexico.
It is listed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in the element “Mariachi, string music, song and trumpet” (inscribed 2011, as recorded on Wikidata).

traditions.intro: Annual tribute of the Passion of Jesus Christ in Iztapalapa, Mexico City.

origins.text: The Passion Play of Iztapalapa, held every Holy Week in a borough of Mexico City, is one of the oldest and best-known passion plays in Mexico. It began not in colonial times but with a procession asking for relief from a 19th-century cholera epidemic. Today it involves hundreds of actors and thousands of ‘Nazarenes’ who carry their own crosses behind the actor playing Jesus.

It is listed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in the element “Representation of the Passion, Death and Resurrection of Christ in Iztapalapa” (inscribed 2025, as recorded on Wikidata).

origins.text: The Huaconada is a ritual dance of Mito, a village in the central Andes of Peru. On the first three days of each January, masked men called huacones dance in the village centre: some in traditional costume and finely carved masks meant to inspire respect, others in modern dress portraying fear, sadness or mockery, all keeping time to a small drum, the tinya.
It is listed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in the element “Huaconada, ritual dance of Mito” (inscribed 2010, as recorded on Wikidata).

origins.text: Attiéké is a dish made from fermented, grated cassava pulp, popular in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana; dried, it has a texture like couscous. It is listed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in the element “Skills related to Attiéké production in Côte d’Ivoire” (inscribed 2024, as recorded on Wikidata).

nativeNames.note: From Wikidata; confirm spelling and language with the community.

traditions.summary: A tradition of India.

origins.text: Mysore silk is a mulberry silk from Mysore in Karnataka. Silk-making in the region, which had declined after the fall of the Vijayanagara Empire, was revived under Tipu Sultan in the late 18th century. Today it is closely tied to the Karnataka Silk Industries Corporation, whose Mysore factory — founded in 1912 by Nalvadi Krishnaraja Wodeyar — weaves silk saris and other garments.
“Mysore silk” is registered in India as a Geographical Indication (handicraft) for Karnataka, application no. 11, 2004–05.

traditions.name: Nakshi kantha
traditions.tagline: A Geographical Indication of West Bengal, India.
traditions.summary: A type of embroidered quilt.
traditions.intro: A type of embroidered quilt.

origins.text: Nakshi kantha is an embroidered quilt, a centuries-old art of the Bengal region — Bangladesh and the Indian states of West Bengal, Tripura and parts of Assam. Made from layers of old cloth and thread, it takes its name from the Bengali word naksha, ‘pattern’. Early kanthas were white, embroidered in red, blue and black.
“Nakshi Kantha” is registered in India as a Geographical Indication (handicraft) for West Bengal, application no. 52, 2007–08.

traditions.name: Nowruz

nativeNames.note: From Wikidata; confirm spelling and language with the community.

traditions.summary: Traditional folk spring festival observed in several countries in Asia and the Middle East.
traditions.intro: Traditional folk spring festival observed in several countries in Asia and the Middle East.

origins.text: Nowruz, meaning ‘new day’, is the Iranian New Year, falling on the spring equinox — usually between 19 and 22 March. Rooted in Zoroastrian tradition and observed for more than 3,000 years, it is now celebrated across West, Central and South Asia, the Caucasus, the Black Sea region and the Balkans, mostly as a secular holiday.

It is listed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in the element “Nawrouz, Novruz, Nowrouz, Nowrouz, Nawrouz, Nauryz, Nooruz, Nowruz, Navruz, Nevruz, Nowruz, Navruz” (inscribed 2016, as recorded on Wikidata).

traditions.name: Paithani
traditions.tagline: A Geographical Indication of Maharashtra, India.

nativeNames.note: From Wikidata; confirm spelling and language with the community.

traditions.summary: Variety of sari.
traditions.intro: Variety of sari.

origins.text: The Paithani is a handwoven silk sari named after Paithan, near Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar in Maharashtra, where it was first made; today the town of Yeola in Nashik district is its largest producer. It is known for borders of oblique square designs and an end-piece (padar) with peacocks, and for kaleidoscope effects created by weaving with one colour lengthwise and another across.
“Paithani sarees and fabrics” is registered in India as a Geographical Indication (handicraft) for Maharashtra, application no. 150 & 153, 2010–11.

origins.text: Pattachitra is traditional scroll painting on cloth from Odisha, West Bengal and parts of Bangladesh, known for fine detail and for its mythological stories and folk tales. In Odisha it was first made for ritual use and as souvenirs for pilgrims to Puri and other temples; in Bengal, painted scrolls were used to illustrate songs as they were sung.

origins.text: Ramlila, ‘Rama's play’, is the folk re-enactment of the life of Rama from the Ramayana and works based on it, such as the Ramcharitmanas. Thousands of performances are staged during the autumn festival of Navaratri, building up to Dussehra night, when giant effigies of Ravana are burnt, often with fireworks.

It is listed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in the element “Ramlila, the traditional performance of the Ramayana” (inscribed 2008, as recorded on Wikidata).

traditions.name: Sambalpuri saree
traditions.tagline: A Geographical Indication of Odisha, India.

nativeNames.note: From Wikidata; confirm spelling and language with the community.

origins.text: The Sambalpuri sari is a handwoven ikat (bandha) sari from western Odisha — Sambalpur, Bargarh, Balangir, Boudh and Sonepur districts — in which the warp and weft threads are tie-dyed before weaving. It carries motifs with deep meaning in Odia culture, such as the conch (shankha), wheel (chakra) and flower (phula), often in red, black and white, the colours associated with Lord Jagannath.
“Sambalpuri bandha saree and fabrics” is registered in India as a Geographical Indication (handicraft) for Odisha, application no. 208, 2012–13.

traditions.name: Tholu bommalata
traditions.tagline: A Geographical Indication of Andhra Pradesh, India.
traditions.summary: Shadow puppet theatre of Andhra Pradesh, India.
traditions.intro: Shadow puppet theatre of Andhra Pradesh, India.

origins.text: Tholu bommalata is the shadow-puppet theatre of Andhra Pradesh, with roots traced as far back as the 3rd century BCE. Its performers belonged to groups of travelling entertainers who moved from village to village through the year, and the art long enjoyed royal patronage. Before radio, film and television, its performances carried the old epics to village audiences.
“Andhra Pradesh leather puppetry” is registered in India as a Geographical Indication (handicraft) for Andhra Pradesh, application no. 107, 2008–09.

origins.text: The Tirupati laddu is the sweet given as prasadam at the Venkateswara Temple in Tirumala, Andhra Pradesh. First introduced in 1715, it grew out of an earlier sweet called manoharam and is made in the temple kitchen by more than 600 people, including skilled cooks called pachakas.

traditions.name: Muga silk
traditions.tagline: A Geographical Indication of Assam, India.
traditions.summary: Variety of wild silk from the cocoons of Antheraea Assama.
traditions.intro: Variety of wild silk from the cocoons of Antheraea Assama.

origins.text: Muga is a wild silk of Assam, known for its natural golden-yellow colour, glossy shimmer and great durability; it was once reserved for royalty. It comes from the Assam silkmoth, whose larvae feed on the aromatic leaves of the som and sualu trees in the Brahmaputra Valley. Its lustre is said to grow with every wash.
“Muga silk of Assam” is registered in India as a Geographical Indication (handicraft) for Assam, application no. 55, 2007–08.

traditions.name: Pashmina
traditions.tagline: A Geographical Indication of Jammu and Kashmir, India.

traditions.intro: Regional name in Ladakh and Kashmir for the fine wool of the cashmere goat.

origins.text: Pashmina is fine cashmere wool from the Changthangi goat — pashm is Persian for ‘wool’ — and, by extension, the Kashmir shawls woven from it. In Kashmir the word meant the raw, unspun wool of these goats. Today ‘pashmina’ can mean either the fibre or the shawl.
“Kashmir Pashmina” is registered in India as a Geographical Indication (handicraft) for Jammu and Kashmir, application no. 46, 2008–09.

origins.text: The rosogolla, or rasgulla — a ‘syrup-filled ball’ — is a dessert of chhena (fresh cheese) dumplings cooked in light sugar syrup. It is agreed to come from the east of the subcontinent, but its exact birthplace is disputed between West Bengal and Odisha, where it is offered at the Jagannath Temple in Puri. Both states now hold Geographical Indications for their own versions.
“Banglar Rasogolla” is registered in India as a Geographical Indication (food stuff) for West Bengal, application no. 533, 2017–18.

traditions.name: Bolon
traditions.summary: Traditional Mandé spike harp with three or four strings and its cultural practices in Mali.
traditions.intro: Traditional Mandé spike harp with three or four strings and its cultural practices in Mali.

origins.text: The bolon, or M'Bolon, is a three-stringed harp of Mali and Guinea, made from a large calabash covered in goatskin with a bow-shaped neck. It was played at hunting ceremonies and before battle to give warriors courage. The player holds it between the legs, plucking the strings and striking the calabash like a drum.

It is listed on UNESCO's List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding in the element “Cultural practices and expressions linked to the 'M’Bolon', a traditional musical percussion instrument” (inscribed 2021, as recorded on Wikidata).

traditions.name: Kôrêdugaw
traditions.summary: Rite of wisdom of the Bambara, Malinké, Senufo and Samogo peoples of Mali.
traditions.intro: Rite of wisdom of the Bambara, Malinké, Senufo and Samogo peoples of Mali.

origins.text: The kôrêdugaw are sacred clowns of Mali, part of secret societies such as the Kore society of the Bambara people. Through deliberately outrageous behaviour — gluttony, mockery and bawdy humour — they teach morality and wisdom, and they also give advice and settle disputes. They perform in the streets, dancing and leading crowds through neighbourhoods.

It is listed on UNESCO's List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding in the element “Secret society of the Kôrêdugaw, the rite of wisdom in Mali” (inscribed 2011, as recorded on Wikidata).

traditions.name: Vimbuza
traditions.summary: Type of dance.
traditions.intro: Type of dance.

origins.text: Vimbuza is a healing dance of the Tumbuka people of northern Malawi, also found among related communities in eastern Zambia and southern Tanzania. The word covers the spirits believed to cause certain illnesses and the drumming, singing and all-night dancing used to identify and calm them. It took its present form in the 19th and early 20th centuries and survived a colonial ban in the 1920s.
It is listed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in the element “Vimbuza healing dance” (inscribed 2008, as recorded on Wikidata).

traditions.name: Durbar festival
traditions.summary: Annual festival celebrated in several cities of Nigeria.
traditions.intro: Annual festival celebrated in several cities of Nigeria.

origins.text: The Durbar is a yearly religious, cultural and equestrian festival at the heart of Hausa culture in northern Nigeria, with roots going back centuries in the Hausa kingdoms. It is held in the old emirate cities — among them Kano, Katsina, Sokoto, Zazzau, Bauchi, Bida and Ilorin — after Ramadan and at the Eid festivals, with grand processions of horsemen.
It is listed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in the element “Durbar in Kano” (inscribed 2024, as recorded on Wikidata).

traditions.name: Kwagh-Hir
traditions.summary: Nigerian Tiv people cultural art.
traditions.intro: Nigerian Tiv people cultural art.

origins.text: Kwagh-hir, ‘a thing of magic’, is a performance art of the Tiv people of central Nigeria that became popular in the 1960s. Combining puppetry, masquerade, poetry, music, dance and storytelling, it tells moral tales about the past and present — to teach, entertain and comment on society. It grew from kwagh-alom, the Tiv tradition of family storytelling.
It is listed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in the element “Kwagh-Hir theatrical performance” (inscribed 2019, as recorded on Wikidata).

nativeNames.note: From Wikidata; confirm spelling and language with the community.

traditions.summary: Group of rituals practised as part of marriage ceremonies mainly in Sudan.
traditions.intro: Group of rituals practised as part of marriage ceremonies mainly in Sudan.

origins.text: Jirtig is a group of rituals performed mainly at weddings, and less often at boys' circumcisions, in central and northern Sudan along the Nile. Rooted in ancient Sudanese tradition, its rites are meant to protect the couple and bring fertility and abundance. It is especially popular among Nubian peoples such as the Danagla, Ja'aliyin, Rubatab, Manasir and Shaigiya.

It is listed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in the element “Al-Jertiq: practices, rituals and expressions for preservation, protection, abundance and fertility in Sudan” (inscribed 2025, as recorded on Wikidata).

nativeNames.note: From Wikidata; confirm spelling and language with the community.

traditions.summary: Traditional dish from West Africa.
traditions.intro: Traditional dish from West Africa.

origins.text: Thieboudienne (ceebu jën in Wolof) is Senegal's national dish: fish, broken rice and tomato sauce cooked together in one pot, often with onions, carrots, cabbage, cassava, hot pepper and lime. Related rice dishes are eaten across West and Central Africa, with meat (tiep yappa) or chicken (tiep ganaar) instead of fish.
It is listed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in the element “Ceebu Jën, a culinary art of Senegal” (inscribed 2021, as recorded on Wikidata).

traditions.name: Bigwala
traditions.summary: Cultural practice of the Basoga people of Uganda, performed during royal celebrations.
traditions.intro: Cultural practice of the Basoga people of Uganda, performed during royal celebrations.

origins.text: Bigwala is the ceremonial gourd-trumpet music and dance of the Busoga Kingdom in Uganda. A solo trumpet is joined by four or more others that build a melody by interlocking single notes (hocketing), then by singers and dancers who circle the players. Once played at royal coronations and funerals, it is now rare, with only a few older masters left.

It is listed on UNESCO's List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding in the element “Bigwala, gourd trumpet music and dance of the Busoga Kingdom in Uganda” (inscribed 2012, as recorded on Wikidata).

traditions.name: ‘ie toga

nativeNames.note: From Wikidata; confirm spelling and language with the community.

alternateNames: 'Ie Samoa, fine mat and its cultural value
traditions.summary: Samoan mat.
traditions.intro: Samoan mat.

origins.text: The ʻie tōga is a finely woven mat of great cultural value in Samoa — called a ‘fine mat’ in English, though it is never used as one. Made by women, and prized for the fineness of the weave and the softness and sheen of the fibre, it has an unwoven fringe and a strip of red feathers. Fine mats are exchanged as gifts at chiefly title bestowals, weddings and funerals.
It is listed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in the element “'Ie Samoa, fine mat and its cultural value” (inscribed 2019, as recorded on Wikidata).

traditions.name: Mbira
traditions.summary: Family of African lamellophones with metal or wooden tines on a resonating body, plucked with thumbs and fingers; especially associated with the Shona people of Zimbabwe, where it holds deep spiritual significance.
traditions.intro: Family of African lamellophones with metal or wooden tines on a resonating body, plucked with thumbs and fingers; especially associated with the Shona people of Zimbabwe, where it holds deep spiritual significance.

origins.text: The mbira is a family of instruments made of a wooden board — often with a resonator — fitted with staggered metal tines that are plucked with the thumbs and fingers. It is traditional to the Shona people of Zimbabwe, and related instruments are played across eastern and southern Africa.

It is listed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in the element “Art of crafting and playing Mbira/Sansi, the finger-plucking traditional musical instrument in Malawi and Zimbabwe” (inscribed 2020, as recorded on Wikidata).

places.name: Northern Rajasthan
places.note: Exact Rajasthan coverage of the GI is unclear

communities.name: Charmakar leather-working communities
communities.description: Leather-working caste groups of Maharashtra and Karnataka with whom the making of Kolhapuri chappals is predominantly associated, then and now.

communities.name: Women painters of Mithila
communities.description: Women of the Mithila region, across several caste communities, who painted the walls and floors of homes for rituals and weddings. Early accounts centred Brahmin and Kayastha styles and overlooked others.

communities.name: Women of undivided Punjab
communities.description: Women across Punjab — a region now divided between India and Pakistan — who embroidered phulkari and bagh for family and ceremonial use.

communities.name: Warli (Varli) Adivasi community
communities.description: An Adivasi (Indigenous) community of the coastal and hill districts on the Maharashtra–Gujarat border, whose ritual wall painting is known as Warli painting.

communities.name: Khatri dyer-printer communities
communities.description: Families of dyers and block-printers in Sindh and Kutch (and in Barmer) associated with ajrakh. Many Kutch families trace their origins to Sindh.

communities.name: Bedouin women of rural UAE communities
communities.description: Women who spin, dye and weave Al Sadu, learning by watching and through gatherings of weavers; men traditionally shear the animals.

organizations.name: LIDCOM — Sant Rohidas Leather Industries & Charmakar Development Corporation
organizations.role: Government of Maharashtra undertaking; reported as a registered proprietor of the Kolhapuri Chappal GI and a signatory to the 2025 agreement with Prada.

organizations.name: LIDKAR — Dr. Babu Jagjivan Ram Leather Industries Development Corporation
organizations.role: Government of Karnataka undertaking; reported as a registered proprietor of the Kolhapuri Chappal GI and a signatory to the 2025 agreement with Prada.

organizations.name: Central Leather Research Institute (CSIR)
organizations.role: Named as applicant on the GI Registry record for Kolhapuri Chappal (Application No. 169).

organizations.name: Maharashtra Chamber of Commerce, Industry & Agriculture (MACCIA)
organizations.role: Raised the attribution complaint with Prada in June 2025 and facilitated the July 2025 artisan visit.

organizations.name: Directorate of Industries, Government of Bihar
organizations.role: Applicant for the Madhubani Paintings GI (Application No. 37).

organizations.name: Mithila Museum, Tokamachi (Niigata, Japan)
organizations.role: Private museum founded by Tokio Hasegawa in 1982, holding one of the largest collections of Mithila painting outside India.

organizations.name: Punjab Small Industries & Export Corporation
organizations.role: Applicant for the Phulkari GI (Application No. 27).

organizations.name: Philadelphia Museum of Art

organizations.name: Victoria and Albert Museum
organizations.role: Holds phulkari in its textile collections.

organizations.name: Adivasi Yuva Seva Sangh / AYUSH (Adivasi Yuva Shakti)

relationships.title: One name, two states
relationships.description: The Kolhapuri Chappal GI covers four districts in Maharashtra and four in Karnataka — a craft shared across a state border.

relationships.title: To the Milan runway
relationships.description: Sandals widely recognised as Kolhapuri in style appear in Prada's Men's SS26 show as 'leather sandals'; inspiration is acknowledged after criticism.

relationships.title: Back to the workshops
relationships.description: A Prada technical team visits Kolhapur's chappal cluster and meets artisans.

relationships.title: An agreement signed in Mumbai
relationships.description: Prada signs an MoU with LIDCOM and LIDKAR for a limited collection made in India, launched in 2026.

relationships.title: Into a museum in Toronto
relationships.description: A late-20th-century Kolhapur chappal on display at the Bata Shoe Museum, labelled by place.

relationships.title: One region, two countries
relationships.description: The Mithila cultural region spans northern Bihar and Nepal's Madhesh around Janakpur.

relationships.title: From walls to paper
relationships.description: A 1960s drought-relief programme of the All India Handicrafts Board brings Mithila painting onto paper and to national markets.

relationships.title: A museum in Japan
relationships.description: Tokio Hasegawa founds the Mithila Museum in Tokamachi, Niigata, and builds a decades-long relationship with Mithila painters.

relationships.title: Punjab, divided in 1947
relationships.description: Phulkari belongs to undivided Punjab and is shared by India and Pakistan.

relationships.title: Philadelphia, 2017
relationships.description: The first major US exhibition of phulkari, which also placed it beside contemporary fashion.

relationships.title: Magiciens de la Terre
relationships.description: Jivya Soma Mashe's Warli painting is exhibited at the Centre Pompidou.

relationships.title: Khatri families from Sindh
relationships.description: Kutch printing families trace their roots to Sindh; accounts of when they moved differ (16th century to about 400 years ago).

relationships.title: After the 2001 earthquake
relationships.description: Printing families move from Dhamadka to the new settlement of Ajrakhpur near Bhuj.

relationships.title: Printed in Barmer too
relationships.description: Ajrakh is also printed in Barmer, Rajasthan. Details of the relationship between centres need documenting.

relationships.title: The 'priest-king' robe
relationships.description: A trefoil-patterned robe on a Mohenjo-daro sculpture resembles some ajrakh motifs. Resemblance is not evidence of continuous tradition, and we do not present it as influence.

relationships.title: A UAE decision taken in India
relationships.description: UNESCO's 20th committee session, in New Delhi, transfers Al Sadu to the Representative List.

trails.title: Crafted by Hand
trails.intro: Four traditions, four sets of hands: stitching leather, printing and dyeing, spinning and weaving, darning in silk. Follow the making, not just the made.

steps.note: Darned from the back of the cloth.

trails.title: Threads Across Borders
trails.intro: Three traditions that modern borders cut through — Punjab, Sindh and Kutch, Mithila. None of them can be filed under one country without losing part of its story.

steps.note: Sindh to Kutch, and back again in every print.

trails.title: Tradition Meets the Runway
trails.intro: When craft enters fashion, what travels — and what is left behind? One documented case, one museum, one market in flux.

steps.note: Milan, June 2025: inspiration acknowledged after the fact.
Philadelphia, 2017: museum and fashion side by side.

trails.title: From Walls to Paper
trails.intro: Two painting traditions made for walls and rituals, which moved onto paper in the 20th century — and turned anonymous painters into named artists.

steps.note: A drought, a programme, a market.
